claim: In the 10th and 11th centuries new towns were founded and existing ones grew in area and population; they were usually enclosed within a wall.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "In the 10th and 11th centuries new cities were founded and existing cities increased in area and population. They were usually enclosed within a wall." Britannica City also describes sustained urban growth after the raids ended. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Europe/Growth-and-innovation https://www.britannica.com/topic/city)

claim: A medieval commune was a self-governing town whose citizens swore an oath of mutual help; it was originally chartered by a bishop, count or king.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "the sworn commune, or the self-regulating city government, originally chartered by a bishop, count, or king". Britannica commune summary: a town with self-governing institutions defined by an oath binding citizens to mutual protection. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Europe/Growth-and-innovation https://www.britannica.com/summary/commune-medieval-Western-Europe)

claim: Emperor Henry V affirmed the principle "Stadtluft macht frei" ("city air brings freedom") in charters for the towns of Speyer and Worms.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica City: "the emperor Henry V affirmed the principle Stadtluft macht frei (German: 'City air brings freedom') in charters for Speyer and Worms". Historische Zeitschrift (2012) on Henry V's Speyer privileges of 1111. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/city https://doi.org/10.1524/hzhz.2012.0558)

claim: New towns founded on lords' lands offered freedom and land to settlers who lived there for more than a year and a day.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica City: new towns "offered freedom and land to settlers who took up residence for more than 'a year and a day.'" Wikipedia Stadtluft macht frei: customary law freed a serf who lived in a city a year and a day. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/city https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadtluft_macht_frei)

claim: Henry V was Holy Roman emperor from 1111 to 1125.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "Holy Roman emperor (1111-25)". Wikipedia Henry V, Holy Roman Emperor: emperor from 1111 until his death in 1125. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-V-Holy-Roman-emperor https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor)

claim: In medieval England and Wales a market was held once a week, on a set day and in a set place.
fact_check_evidence: IHR Gazetteer: a market was held "once a week, on a set day and in a set place". Kent Archaeological Society on market establishment 1086-1350 describes weekly chartered markets. (https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/intro.html https://www.kentarchaeology.org.uk/journal/117/factors-market-establishment-medieval-england-evidence-kent-1086-1350)

claim: In medieval England a royal charter gave a town, village, monastery or other religious house the right to hold a regular market.
fact_check_evidence: Historic England: "A royal charter for markets was a document issued by the monarch granting a town, village, monastic house or religious foundation the right to hold regular markets." IHR Gazetteer lists royal grants of markets from 1199. (https://heritagecalling.com/2024/03/14/the-timeless-charm-of-english-market-towns-and-halls/ https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/intro.html)

claim: From 1200, English royal grants allowed a new market or fair only if it did not harm neighbouring markets or fairs.
fact_check_evidence: IHR Gazetteer: from 1200 royal charters granted "the right to hold a market or fair only if this was not detrimental to neighbouring markets or fairs." The Gazetteer full introduction repeats the condition. (https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/intro.html https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/fullintro.html)

claim: A medieval fair was held once a year on a set date, usually a saint's feast day, and could last from one day to a week or more.
fact_check_evidence: IHR Gazetteer: fairs were annual, "held on a set date, normally associated with the feast of a particular saint", lasting from one day to a week or more. Wikipedia Charter fair: annual fairs often tied to a saint's day. (https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/intro.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_fair)

claim: The Champagne fairs rotated among four towns, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, and reached their peak in the 13th century.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica names fairs at Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, reaching their apogee in the 13th century. Wikipedia Champagne fairs: an annual circuit of six fairs in these four towns. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Champagne-fair https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_fairs)

claim: At the Champagne fairs, protected by the count's privilege, northern cloth was exchanged for spices and dyes from Mediterranean lands.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: exchange of "northern cloth for spices and dyes from Mediterranean lands", traders "favoured by the count's privilege". Wikipedia Champagne fairs: textiles, leather, fur and spices; the counts' Guards of the Fair. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Champagne-fair https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_fairs)

claim: Deals at the Champagne fairs often used letters of credit, laying groundwork for modern credit.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "Transactions often involved letters of credit, laying the groundwork for modern credit systems." Wikipedia Champagne fairs describes the fairs as a clearing house for credit and exchange. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Champagne-fair https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_fairs)

claim: Piepowder courts, named from the French for "dusty feet", settled disputes at English fairs and markets quickly and on the spot.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: the name derives from the dusty feet of the participants; the court decided disputes arising in fairs and markets summarily and on the spot. Wikipedia Court of piepowders agrees. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/piepoudre-court https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_piepowders)

claim: Merchant guilds grouped the merchants of a town; craft guilds grouped the artisans of one branch of industry or trade.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: merchant guilds were associations of all or most of a town's merchants; craft guilds comprised the artisans in a particular branch of industry or commerce. Wikipedia Guild draws the same distinction. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/guild-trade-association https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild)

claim: Craft guilds arose soon after merchant guilds, in expanding towns where an extensive division of labour was emerging.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: craft guilds "originated in expanding towns in which an extensive division of labour was emerging." Wikipedia Guild links craft guilds to growing medieval towns. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/guild-trade-association https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild)

claim: Guilds held a monopoly of trade in their town or branch of industry, set standards for the quality of goods and worked to keep prices stable.

claim: A guild often had a patron saint and kept a chapel in the parish church; guilds also did charitable work and built guildhalls.

fact_check_evidence: Britannica: a guild was often associated with a patron saint and maintained a chapel in the parish church; guilds performed charitable work and built guildhalls. claim: The "journey" in journeyman originally meant a day's labour: journeymen worked for wages, often paid by the day.

claim: A journeyman who proved his technical skill with a "masterpiece" might rise to become a master.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "A journeyman who could provide proof of his technical competence (the 'masterpiece') might rise in the guild to the status of a master." claim: In a medieval castle, bakers made fine white wheat rolls for the lady's table and rough loaves of barley, oats or even peas and beans for servants.
fact_check_evidence: English Heritage: "fine white wheat rolls for the lady's table to rough loaves made from barley, oats or even peas and beans for servants". Wikipedia Medieval cuisine: barley, oat and rye among the poor, wheat for the governing classes. claim: At medieval feasts food was often served on slices of bread that caught the juices, and eaten with the fingers; forks did not appear on medieval tables.
fact_check_evidence: UWM (Martha Carlin): food "served on top of slices of bread to catch the juices, and they were eaten with the fingers"; "Forks did not appear on medieval tables." Wikipedia Trencher: stale bread used as a plate. (https://uwm.edu/news/feasting-in-medieval-england-pottage-boiled-beef-and-no-forks/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trencher_(tableware))

claim: Meat on the table was a sign of status; peasants ate it only rarely, mainly before winter, when livestock was culled so fewer animals had to be fed through winter.
fact_check_evidence: English Heritage: "It was meat on the table that was an indicator of status in the medieval period, with the peasantry eating it only rarely, and then mainly in the run-up to winter". Wikipedia Medieval cuisine: meat was more prestigious and costly. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/members-area/members-magazine/feasts-stokesay/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_cuisine)

claim: Religious fasting banned meat on Fridays and many other days of the year, so fish took its place.
fact_check_evidence: English Heritage: fish replaced meat "on Fridays and many other days throughout the year". UWM (Martha Carlin): meat-eating was prohibited on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays as religious fasting. (https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/castles/life-in-a-castle/ https://uwm.edu/news/feasting-in-medieval-england-pottage-boiled-beef-and-no-forks/)

claim: At medieval feasts, lower-ranking diners got coarser bread and second-quality ale, while wine was expensive because it was imported.
fact_check_evidence: UWM: servants got "coarser bread, second-quality ale and no wine"; "spices and wine were very expensive because they were all imported." English Heritage Stokesay: more ale for those lower in rank. (https://uwm.edu/news/feasting-in-medieval-england-pottage-boiled-beef-and-no-forks/ https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/members-area/members-magazine/feasts-stokesay/)

claim: Spices were costly imports, and lords served strong-tasting sauces made with expensive foreign spices to show off their wealth.
fact_check_evidence: English Heritage: "strong-tasting sauces, using expensive foreign spices" displayed the lord's wealth. UWM: spices were very expensive because imported. Yale University Press on Freedman: spices were symbols of affluence. claim: Spices were costly imports, and lords served strong-tasting sauces made with expensive foreign spices to show off their wealth.

claim: Historians reject the idea that spices hid rotten meat: spices cost far more than fresh meat, and salting and smoking preserved food better.
fact_check_evidence: Reviews of Freedman's Out of the East: he calls the spoiled-meat idea a false urban legend; the price of spices far exceeded that of fresh meat, and salting, pickling or smoking preserved better. Medievalists.net: spices were far too expensive to waste on bad meat. (https://www.medievalists.net/2014/06/spoiled-splendid-speculations-culinary-misgiving/ https://www.economics.utoronto.ca/munro5/MunroFreedmanAHR09.pdf)

claim: In 14th-century England wool was the most commonly bought fabric, from cheap russet and blanket to costly scarlet; linen came second.
fact_check_evidence: Silverman (Ohio State): wool fabrics "the most commonly purchased fabric, including everything from inexpensive fabrics such as russet and blanket to the far more expensive scarlet woolens"; linen second. Wikipedia Russet (cloth): a coarse, cheap wool. (https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=osu1322596483&disposition=inline https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russet_(cloth))

claim: Pointed shoes called poulaines were a late-medieval fashion; in 1463 King Edward IV limited their toe points in London to under two inches.
fact_check_evidence: University of Cambridge: "in 1463 King Edward IV passed a law limiting toe-point length to less than two inches within London." Smithsonian Magazine: Edward IV's 1463 laws limited toe length to two inches. claim: Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th, and linked the rise to pointed shoes.
fact_check_evidence: University of Cambridge: 6% of individuals from the 11th-13th centuries versus 27% from the 14th-15th centuries, linked to pointed-toe shoes. Smithsonian Magazine reports the same figures. (https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/bunions https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/medieval-europeans-obsession-pointy-shoes-caused-painful-bunions-180977969/)

claim: An English law of 1363 set what cloth people of each social rank could wear, from servants and craftsmen up to merchants and knights.
fact_check_evidence: Silverman (Ohio State): the 1363 law "was put in place to control the consumption of fabrics and related goods based on social class". Wikipedia Statute Concerning Diet and Apparel 1363: dress codes by rank from servants to knights. (https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=osu1322596483&disposition=inline https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_Concerning_Diet_and_Apparel_1363)

claim: The 1363 law blamed the "outrageous and excessive apparel" of people dressing against their "estate and degree".

claim: Under the 1363 law the lowest ranks could wear only blanket and russet, coarse wool cloth worth no more than 12 pence.
fact_check_evidence: Silverman (Ohio State): russet and blanket, coarse wools named in the 1363 law for the lowest class, at "not more than twelve pence". claim: Sumptuary laws have proved difficult or impossible to enforce over the long term.

claim: In 1086 a royal survey recorded more than 5,000 water mills in England south of the Severn and Trent rivers.

claim: The earliest-known references to windmills come from Persia, in the years 644 and 915.

fact_check_evidence: Wikipedia (Fall of Constantinople): a watershed of the Late Middle Ages; quotes Britannica that many scholars see it as marking the end of the Middle Ages. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople)

claim: In 1517 Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg began the Reformation, which reshaped Western Christianity.
fact_check_evidence: Wikipedia (Ninety-five Theses): retrospectively considered to have launched the Protestant Reformation. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses)

claim: Luther's ideas were printed and reprinted within weeks and read across Europe; print was the catalyst of the Reformation.
fact_check_evidence: Wikipedia (Ninety-five Theses): the theses were quickly printed and widely copied, one of the first controversies aided by the printing press. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses)

claim: Eyeglasses were first made in Italy, most probably in Pisa, around 1290; the first ones had convex lenses to help farsighted people.
fact_check_evidence: Medievalists.net: eyeglasses invented in Italy in the 1280s; Britannica: in Europe eyeglasses first appeared in Italy, with convex lenses for farsightedness. (https://www.medievalists.net/2016/03/medieval-eyeglasses-wearable-technology-of-the-thirteenth-century/ https://www.britannica.com/science/eyeglasses)

claim: In a sermon of 1306, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making eyeglasses was not yet twenty years old, and that he had spoken to its discoverer.
fact_check_evidence: Medievalists.net quotes Fra Giordano's 1306 sermon: 'It is not twenty years since there was discovered the art of making spectacles'. (https://www.medievalists.net/2016/03/medieval-eyeglasses-wearable-technology-of-the-thirteenth-century/)

claim: The first clearly recorded mechanical clocks were large weight-driven machines in towers; they struck the hours rather than showing them. England's oldest surviving one, at Salisbury Cathedral, dates from 1386.
fact_check_evidence: Wikipedia (Salisbury Cathedral clock): a large iron-framed tower clock without a dial, dated to about 1386, whose purpose was to strike a bell. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Cathedral_clock)

claim: The word clock comes from Medieval Latin clocca, 'bell'.
fact_check_evidence: Wikipedia (Clock): the word clock derives from the medieval Latin word for bell, clocca. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock)
